title: Best AI/workflow for pixel art characters and animations?
author: Incerceron
selftext:
I’m a solo developer making a 2D game with AI support, and I’m struggling with pixel art characters.

I need 64x64 characters with 4 directions and animations like idle, walk, and attack. I tried tools like [PixelLab.ai](http://PixelLab.ai) and GPT Image, but I keep getting problems like wrong attack directions, inconsistent frames, and unusable sprite sheets.

I’m also not very good at manually editing pixel art, so I can’t rely on heavy cleanup frame by frame.

The bigger issue is scalability: eventually I may need 20–30+ characters, so I’m not just looking for a way to make one character — I need a workflow I can keep using.

For now, Universal LPC Character Generator feels more reliable, but also a bit limiting.

So I wanted to ask:

* Which AI tools would you recommend for this?
* Is there any good workflow for consistent 64x64 character animation?
* Or is a hybrid approach (like LPC + small manual edits) currently the best option?

I’m open to suggestions.

comments.author: HugoDzz
comments.body: Still WIP, but I've made [my own](https://www.spritefusion.com/pixel-art-gallery) model

replies.author: Incerceron
replies.body:
I tried Sprite Fusion and it actually worked surprisingly well — it generated a usable right-facing crossbow attack animation on the first try.  
My main concern is the credit cost though. One animation costs 15 credits, while the Creator plan only gives 1,050 credits/month. Since I’ll eventually need 20–30+ characters with multiple directions and animations, that can add up very quickly.  
Do you use Sprite Fusion for your whole pipeline, or is there a way you reduce the number of generations/credit usage?

replies.author: HugoDzz
replies.body:
Thanks! Yes I do use it for all my games and anything pixel art, I’m very picky on the quality so I dogfood my own tools!

For costs, I try to optimize a lot, but it’s not enough to me as well.

replies.author: Incerceron
replies.body: Thanks, that’s really helpful. Sprite Fusion gave me one of the best results I’ve had so far, so I’ll probably keep testing it despite the credit cost. Hopefully they improve the pricing or credit limits at some point. If you have any tips for getting more consistent results with fewer generations, I’d love to hear them.

replies.author: HugoDzz
replies.body: I tend to use the style reference mode a lot, like asking for « dungeon props in the same style ». So it gives me multiple props at once, instead of asking for a chest, then for a candle etc.

replies.body: Thanks! I joined the Discord and asked in the workflow channel. Hopefully I can find a pipeline that works well for this.

comments.author: Little_Grimmy_Reap
comments.body:
I’ve been using codex astra with aseprite Mcp all plugged into godot mcp,

With enough tweaking and feedback you can get some solid pixel animations. I’ve even fed it official academic videos of athletes for reference.

For example I fed it a video of someone dual wielding wakezashi and it got the stance and swings pretty solid. Also did this for historical greatsword usage and it nailed it - 8 directions with running and idles

comments.author: magicdoorai
comments.body: For 20–30 characters, I'd treat LPC (or another fixed template) as the production rig and use image generation mainly for character concepts/reference. Lock the 64×64 canvas, pivot point, palette/outline rules, and frame grid once. Build one clean 4-direction idle/walk/attack sheet, then vary reusable layers (body, hair, clothes, equipment) instead of generating every frame independently. A quick flipbook/overlay check on each export will catch jitter and wrong facing before it gets into the game. If manual cleanup is your bottleneck, a small library of reusable parts is likely to scale better than chasing a model that makes a perfect full sheet in one pass.
